## Particle kinematics {.title-card}

::: {.subtitle}
KT1 · 2026 · Lecture 2
:::

Energy, momentum and reconstructed mass.

::: {.notes}
Draft assembled from material deferred from Lecture 1. Add the full covariant/contravariant and metric teaching sequence before presenting.
:::

## Energy units and four-momentum

An **electronvolt** (eV) is the energy gained by charge $e$ across a potential difference of one volt.

$$1\,\mathrm{GeV}=10^9\,\mathrm{eV}.$$

The **four-momentum** combines energy $E$ and three-momentum $\mathbf p$:

$$p^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf p),\qquad E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^4.$$

We will use units with $c=1$.

::: {.notes}
Introduce m as rest mass and c as the speed of light. In natural units energies, masses and momenta are expressed in GeV; with c restored their units differ. The invariant norm uses the (+,−,−,−) metric. State this relation without deriving it here.
:::



## Can we find a particle that decays unseen?

$$pp\longrightarrow Z+X\longrightarrow\mu^+\mu^-+X$$

Measure the two muons.

Reconstruct the mass of their parent.

[Explore a CMS collision event](https://opendata.cern.ch/visualise/events/cms)

::: {.notes}
X denotes the rest of the event. This is the running example, not a claim that every dimuon pair comes from a Z. Open the CMS display as an optional instructor-led extension; choose a suitable dimuon event before class. The deck does not automatically select an event.
:::



## Symbols for the two-muon measurement

$p_1,p_2$: the measured muon **four-momenta**.  
$E_1,E_2$: their energies.  
$\theta$: the angle between their three-momenta.  
$M$: the reconstructed mass of the pair.

For a pair from one parent, four-momentum conservation gives $p_{\mathrm{parent}}=p_1+p_2$.

::: {.notes}
Clarify four-vectors versus three-vectors before the blackboard expansion. The superscript μ is an index, not the muon symbol. The square of a four-vector is its Minkowski norm, not the sum of four positive squares.
:::



## Two tracks, one mass

In units with $c=1$:

$$M^2=(p_1+p_2)^2.$$

For highly relativistic daughters:

$$M^2\simeq2E_1E_2(1-\cos\theta).$$

**The reconstructed mass is independent of the observer’s frame.**

::: {.notes}
Blackboard, 5–7 minutes, the only derivation. Define p_i=(E_i, p-vector_i) and the (+,−,−,−) metric. Expand M²=(E1+E2)²−|p1+p2|²=m1²+m2²+2(E1E2−p1·p2). For relativistic muons neglect m_mu and use |p_i|≈E_i, giving 2E1E2(1−cosθ). Take two back-to-back muons with E1=E2=45.6 GeV: M≈91.2 GeV. This is an idealized numerical example, not a measured event. Conservation of four-momentum makes the sum the parent four-momentum; its Minkowski norm is invariant. Stop here, without a second derivation of fixed-target kinematics.
:::



## From events to a mass distribution

An **event** is one recorded collision. It gives one value of the reconstructed pair mass.

A **histogram** counts how many events fall within each interval of mass.

A **resonance** can appear as a localized excess near a parent particle’s mass.

Other processes produce **background** events in the same measurement.

::: {.notes}
Finite detector resolution and the particle’s intrinsic decay width both affect a peak. Repeated evidence and controlled uncertainties are necessary. Do not present a schematic peak as actual data.
:::



## A discovery needs many collisions

One pair gives one reconstructed mass.

Many events produce a mass distribution.

A localized excess can reveal a resonance.

**Backgrounds and detector effects must also be tested.**

::: {.notes}
Explain a Z peak near 91 GeV qualitatively. A peak alone is not sufficient proof of a new particle: calibration, background modelling and statistical evidence matter. Cross section describes production frequency, lifetime describes decay, and branching fraction describes the fraction in a given decay channel. Formal calculations come later.
:::




## What is momentum transfer?

$$\mathbf q=\mathbf p_{\mathrm{in}}-\mathbf p_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad Q=|\mathbf q|.$$

$\mathbf p_{\mathrm{in}}$: incoming probe momentum.  
$\mathbf p_{\mathrm{out}}$: outgoing probe momentum.

$\mathbf q$ is the momentum delivered to the target system.

Even a change of direction alone gives a nonzero transfer.

::: {.notes}
This slide defines Q as the magnitude of a three-momentum transfer for a simple spatial-resolution estimate. In relativistic scattering literature Q² often means minus the squared four-momentum transfer; do not silently identify those two definitions. The target system includes any recoiling or produced particles.
:::



## Resolution and momentum transfer

$$R\sim\frac{\hbar}{Q}.$$

$R$: distance scale probed. $Q=|\mathbf q|$: magnitude of the three-momentum transfer in this estimate.

$\hbar=h/(2\pi)$: reduced Planck constant.

A larger transfer can reveal finer structure. High beam momentum alone is insufficient if the deflection is tiny.

::: {.notes}
Order-of-magnitude spatial-resolution estimate, not an exact radius formula. Distinguish this Q from invariant relativistic momentum-transfer conventions.
:::
